newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Treasury sees new 2010 bond in 97/8.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Treasury sees new 2010 bond in 97/8.

text.p: The Australian Treasury will introduce a new benchmark 2010 fixed coupon bond in the second half of the 1997/98 (July-June) fiscal year, and said that further issuance of the November 2006 line was unlikely.
Tony Hinton, First Assistant Secretary of Treasury's Investment and Debt Division, also said Treasury expected the first tender of indexed bonds for the 1997/98 year to be held this month.
Hinton told an Australian Financial Markets Association dinner that Treasury had not revised its debt issue programme of about A$6.5 to A$7.5 billion for 1997/98.
This programme is to comprise around A$5 to A$6 billion of fixed coupon bond issuance, around A$500 million to A$1 billion index bonds, and around A$1 billion of adjustable rate bonds.
Hinton said Treasury would look to build and maintain liquidity in key benchmark bonds, and maintain an efficient and liquid curve out to the present 12 to 13 years.
"Consistent with that, at this stage it is expected that Treasury Bond issuance in 1997/98 will be weighted towards stocks in the long end of the curve," Hinton said.

"We plan, at this stage, to introduce a new 2010 benchmark line to maintain the length of the yield curve and to ensure, in the longer term, that a smooth progression of stocks is available to move into the 10-year futures contract," he said.
The introduction of a 2010 bond this year would allow time for liquidity in the line to build up prior to it becoming the 10-year benchmark, he said.

Given there was a need to build up liquidity in existing long dated bonds, specifically the October 2007, August 2008 and September 2009, the new line would not be introduced until the second half of the financial year, Hinton said.
Further issuance in 1997/98 of the November 2006 stock was unlikely.

Tenders would be held about four to six week intervals. The borrowing requirement meant the average tender size would be A$500 to A$600 million, smaller than the average tender size in recent years, and may only contain one stock.

"In circumstances of a reduced issuance programme, it is possible that, in future, some tenders may only have one stock on offer, particularly where we are looking quickly to build liquidity into particular lines," he said.

Hinton said the indexed bond market had continued to develop over the last year, and that given this development, Treasury feedback had suggested some change to present issuing arrangements was warranted.
Hinton said indexed bond tenders would now be held on a regular six to eight week cycle, with volume and the stock offered depending on market demand and feedback.
"At this stage, we anticipate that the first tender of the 1997/98 Treasury Indexed Bonds issue program will be conducted prior to the end of this month," he said.

Issuance in 1997/98 would initially target the 2020 line, introduced in 1996/97, but Treasury also planned to continue to issue the 2015 line. It was possible both lines could be offered at the same tender, Hinton said.

The impact on Treasury adjustable rate bonds (TABs) of recent changes to prime asset ratio (PAR) requirements would have assessed before Treasury came to any firm views on the make-up of the 1997/98 program, he said.
"Accordingly, the first TABs tender for 1997/98 is not expected to be held until the December quarter," Hinton said.

Given the orignal March 1998 line matured this financial year and the existing October 2000 line, of which there was some A$4.3 billion on issue, now had a matirity of close to three years, Hinton said the possibility of a launching a new TAB during the year was being looked into.

"At this stage, opur thinking is that any new TABs line would probably have a maturity of around five years," Hinton said, although market input would be sought before a final decision was made. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
